items.title: No local account of who leaves the pathway
items.whyItMatters: Patients who stop answering calls lose support when risk is highest, and the clinic cannot say who they are.
items.opportunity: Define disengagement as no contact for six weeks and follow dispensing history, with consent, after disengagement.

items.title: Success defined by a dose threshold
items.whyItMatters: Thresholds from 25 percent to discontinuation made studies impossible to compare and can read as a target for patients.
items.opportunity: Use percent change in dose as the primary outcome and report the proportion reaching 25 percent only descriptively.

items.title: Overdose and emergency visits rarely measured
items.whyItMatters: Only six of 27 studies in the review reported them; a pathway could reduce dose and still cause harm.
items.opportunity: Collect emergency visits and overdose from hospital data for everyone, including those who leave.

items.title: Interpreter need and distance not planned for
items.whyItMatters: Both predicted leaving a supported taper elsewhere (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Record both at entry and report outcomes separately; offer interpreter-supported calls.

items.title: No concurrent comparison
items.whyItMatters: Dose falls over time for many reasons; a single-arm follow-up cannot attribute change to the pathway.
items.opportunity: Describe outcomes honestly as outcomes of pathway patients and compare with published figures only as context.

errorsFound: The planning figure of 58 percent reaching a 25 percent reduction comes from an uncontrolled before-after study and should not be used as an expected effect.
reevaluation: The gaps point to a descriptive prospective follow-up with a continuous dose outcome, deliberate follow-up of people who leave, and safety outcomes for everyone.
summary: Five gaps: unknown disengagement, threshold outcomes, unmeasured harm, equity of access to support, and no comparison group.
